extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for Area Chairs on managing reviewer assignments, moderating discussion, running borderline-paper meetings, writing meta-reviews, handling ethics and revision issues, and making accept/reject recommendations for ICLR 2024 submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three quality reviews per paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Each submission should receive three quality reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs should ensure every submission gets three informed reviews; if the paper lacks 3 informed reviews or assigned reviewers are unresponsive, immediately recruit emergency/additional reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet and recommend reviewer assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs should recommend appropriate reviewers for papers assigned based on AC bids and vet reviewer-paper assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may skip recommending reviewers (in which case reviewers will be assigned by bids), but when assigned reviewers are delinquent or non-responsive, help assign alternate reviewers in a timely manner so every submission is judged fairly and expertly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify delinquent reviewers and assign alternates
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor reviewer responsiveness and replace delinquent reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer is unresponsive after reminders (2-3 reminders suggested), assign an emergency reviewer. Contact SACs or program chairs if you struggle to find replacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision recommendation with meta-review
rubrics_metrics.description: For every submission, ACs must recommend accept or reject accompanied by a meta-review summarizing reviews and discussions and optionally adding their own view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommendation should be justified based on content and discussion. Senior Area Chairs and Program Chairs will help calibrate decisions; AC recommendations are a key input but may be adjusted in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review minimum length
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to write a meta-review of at least 60 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs have full freedom in wording, but authors find summaries of this length useful. Meta-reviews are public and should be clear and constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: describe main content and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-reviews should include a concise description of the submission’s main content (scientific claims and findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both what the paper discusses and what is missing from the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: summarize discussion and responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-reviews should concisely summarize the discussion: list points raised by reviewers, how each point was addressed by authors, and whether the AC found each point worth consideration in decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ICLR has extended discussion, ACs are encouraged to use the meta-review to capture the multi-week back-and-forth and its impact on judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: clear recommendation and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-reviews must end with a clear indication of the AC recommendation, justified based on content and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State accept/reject and provide reasoning tying evidence from reviews, author responses, and any meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize reviewer-AC meetings for borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs are required to organize a virtual meeting with reviewers for each borderline paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect reviewer emails from OpenReview, schedule with a tool (e.g., Doodle), consider time zones, use an online tool (e.g., Jitsi), ask reviewers to prepare, and summarize the meeting in OpenReview. Historically this will be ~3-4 meetings per stack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and handling of borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Borderline papers are identified primarily by review scores and score spread and will be flagged for meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While scores are a proxy, ACs may organize meetings for any papers they consider borderline/worth discussing. Use meetings to resolve disagreements among reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downweight reviews for non-attending reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs may downweight the review of reviewers who refuse to attend required meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers agreed to participate in meetings when accepting invitations; if they fail to attend after reminders, the AC can proceed without them and mark their non-attendance for future reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion moderation: keep discussions constructive and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs must moderate submission discussions, discouraging participation irrelevant to scientific claims and merits and preventing toxicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage polite, constructive language from reviewers and authors; remove or discourage comments that are not about scientific merits, limitations, or clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage reviewers to respond to author rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs should prompt and encourage reviewers to respond to author rebuttals during the discussion period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active engagement helps ensure authors' clarifications are considered in decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate as expert in discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs are expected not only to moderate but also to contribute their own scientific assessment of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors and reviewers for clarifications when needed, present your own view of the paper, and be an active participant rather than a passive moderator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle Code of Ethics flags
rubrics_metrics.description: If any submission, review, or discussion raises ethical concerns, flag the content and contact Program Chairs; collect information and provide evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AC recommendations on ethics-flagged papers are non-binding; flagged papers may be passed to the Ethics board for further review. Carefully consider facts and communicate with program chairs (program-committee@iclr.cc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag papers for desk reject
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs can flag papers for desk rejection when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide information and any evidence used to support the recommendation; note that the AC recommendation may be non-binding and may go to the Ethics board if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to recruit emergency/additional reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek emergency/additional reviewers when assigned reviewers are unresponsive past the deadline or when extra reviews could improve confidence in the recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediately start recruiting if the paper lacks 3 informed reviews. Assign emergency reviewers using the AC console; contact your paired SAC or program chairs if you cannot find reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to direct author messages
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs should promptly respond to reasonable inquiries from authors left as comments addressed to the AC on OpenReview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a question requires higher-level discussion, bring it to the corresponding SACs. Use author messages to help activate or clarify discussion when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of author revisions during discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may revise submissions during the discussion window (dates given); ACs should take revisions into account, but may ignore revisions that are substantially different from the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide states authors can update papers until Nov 22 (and elsewhere notes up to Nov 18); ensure you know the operative deadline. Final decisions and meta-reviews should consider any revisions unless they substantially change the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous work and citation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers are considered contemporaneous if published within two months before the submission deadline; authors are not required to compare to such very recent work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the full paper deadline is Sep 28, 2024, papers published on or after July 28 are not required to be compared against. Authors are encouraged to cite and discuss relevant papers (including non-peer-reviewed arXiv work) but may be excused for not knowing about non-peer-reviewed or very recent works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base decisions on paper quality and reviews, not score curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on a pre-shared rating curve; make accept/reject recommendations based on reviews and paper quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program Chairs will not share the rating curve. SACs can help with calibration if needed; focus on the intrinsic quality of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-reviews are public
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-reviews and AC comments will be publicly available and shared with authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write meta-reviews with that transparency in mind: be clear, constructive, and polite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and language: constructive and polite
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the language used in reviews and meta-reviews is constructive and polite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to suggested reading on constructive criticism (e.g., 'Criticizing with Kindness') and examples of reviewer mistakes to guide tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical meeting organization guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tips for organizing online reviewer-AC meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect reviewer emails from OpenReview, propose potential dates (consider time zones), use scheduling tools (e.g., Doodle), provide an online conferencing tool (e.g., Jitsi), and send reminders. If a majority do not attend after reminders, proceed with available reviewers and inform SACs.
